newsitem.title: FRANCE: Tchuruk kicks Alcatel back into shape.
newsitem.headline: Tchuruk kicks Alcatel back into shape.

text.p: Serge Tchuruk is delivering on the main task he faced when he took over ailing Alcatel Alsthom 15 months ago, kicking the telecoms and industrial power giant back into shape.

Tchuruk, 58, a Frenchman from a Marseilles-based Armenian family called Tchurukdichian, was named chairman in June 1995 to replace Pierre Suard, who had been barred by an anti-corruption judge from running Alcatel

A good public speaker with a reputation for clarity and a decisive mind who came from energy group Total SA, Tchuruk spent the summer of 1995 preparing an overhaul of the firm that also makes France's prestige TGV high-speed trains.
Alcatel had been slow in reacting to a market change and remained until his arrival closely focused on serving traditional monopoly telecoms suppliers in many countries.

The group's weaknesses were highlighted when it fell into the red in 1994 in the face of explosive growth in mobile telecommunications and austerity drives by telecoms operators facing new competition and preparing for full liberalisation of the sector after 1998.
Tchuruk poached Total's former finance director, Jean-Pierre Halbron, from U.S. merchant bank Wasserstein Perella.
The two slimmed down management, reorganised the company along product lines and initiated a two-pronged programme of cost-cuts and asset sales.

For the year 1995, Alcatel made a historically high loss of 26.6 billion french francs ($5.17 billion) after heavy restructuring charges. Some 20,000 people have lost their jobs, mainly in Europe, of the 191,000 employed at the end of 1995.
Where the group consisted of 900 seperate legal entities, Tchuruk aims to cut the number to 500 by the end of 1997.
The company is set to return to the black in 1996 and to what it says will be "good profits" in 1998.
Tchuruk hates complex structures and wants to have clear control.

He sold Alcatel's stake in Italian carmaker Fiat, because it was not a core activity, and the 25 percent stake in mobile telecoms operator Cofira because it handicapped his efforts to supply other operators. Alcatel's actvities in newspapers and magazines were sold to media group Havas.
But at the same time that he was cutting and pruning the company, Tchuruk ambitions for the group remained big. He says he wants to expand despite the company's large debts.

While Suard was a reserved and uncommunicative chairman, Tchuruk talks to journalists and financial analysts in a small well-prepared meetings where he runs the show singlehandedly as if he were a university professor lecturing business students.

At the start of the year, when he announced the company's big losses, he said he wanted to obtain full control of nuclear engineering group Framatome which Suard had tried to capture over many years, without success.
Now the state has agreed to sell the company to the GEC Alsthom joint venture in a deal that will also give Alcatel majority control of GEC Alsthom.

Tchuruk, an arms engineer by training, also surprised the financial markets by announcing he wanted to acquire defence to consumer electronics group Thomson SA from the state. Industry obsevers say Alcatel stands a good chance of winning over rival bidder Lagardere Groupe.
Meanwhile the group concluded technology deals with Sharp Corp of Japan and Motorola of the U.S. ($1=5.145 French Franc)
